Employees who extend a trip for personal reasons must pay for the extra nights themselves.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why Cities Run Hot
quests.passage: On a summer evening, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while tall buildings block cooling breezes. A scarcity of trees makes matters worse, since leaves shade the ground and release water vapor that cools the air. In one study, streets lined with mature trees were up to six degrees cooler than similar streets without them. Planners increasingly favor planting trees and painting roofs white, though a few residents complain that the work causes disruption and that trees can block shop signs.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Last Lesson
quests.passage: Mr. Okafor had taught chemistry for thirty-one years, and on his last day he did what he always did: he wrote the date on the board, checked that the burners were off, and began the lesson. The students, who had planned a small party, waited. Halfway through, he stopped and looked at the clock. "I had a speech prepared," he said. "But I notice it's ten past two, and you have a test tomorrow." Someone groaned. He smiled, picked up the chalk, and carried on. Only when the bell rang did he turn to them, glance at the cake on the back bench, and say, "Now, I think there was something about a party."

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: E-reader or Paperback?
quests.passage: The case for the e-reader is practical: a single device holds hundreds of books, weighs less than a paperback, and lets you enlarge the print. For travelers and readers with poor eyesight, these advantages are real. Paperback defenders, however, point to something harder to measure. They say that a printed book makes it easier to remember where in the story a passage appeared, and that it comes without notifications or the temptation to check messages. There is some evidence for the first claim, but the second depends entirely on self-discipline, since most e-readers do not have notifications at all. The honest conclusion is that neither format is better; each simply suits a different kind of reader.

quests.passage: My father's garage was never organized, but he could always find what he needed. Ask for a particular washer and he would move three boxes, reach behind a shelf, and produce it. As a teenager, I thought this was luck. After he died, I spent a weekend clearing the garage and discovered that nothing was where it looked. Each cluttered shelf hid a small, careful system: screws sorted by length inside old coffee tins, and the tins labeled in pencil on the underside, where only he would look. I did not tidy it in the end. I only added a label of my own, in the same place, in my own handwriting.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why Coffee Costs What It Costs
quests.passageTopic: Why Coffee Costs What It Costs
quests.passage: A cup of coffee at a downtown café may cost twice as much as the same drink two miles away, and the beans are rarely the reason. Rent in busy districts can account for more of the price than the coffee itself, and cafés there must also pay higher wages to attract staff. Owners also consider what customers will accept: commuters buying a drink on the way to work are less price-sensitive than students lingering over a laptop. Some cafés therefore charge for the speed and convenience of the location rather than for the drink. Customers who walk an extra few blocks often find the same coffee for far less, which is why the cheapest cup is rarely the nearest one.
